parents.Gloss: related as brother and sister; brother; sister; relative; female relative, esp. son's wife

proposals.evidence: The brother-in-law lexeme ẓami plausibly continues the jāmí family of CDIAL 5200. Turner directly lists older Dameli žamī under wife’s brother; Savi žamī explicitly covers both wife’s brother and sister’s husband, matching the modern male-ego senses. Compare Kati žämī, Gawarbati žamī and Kalasha ǰōmī. The modern retroflex transcription versus the older spelling requires qualification; the Nuristani comparison does not prove a donor direction. Exclude žami woman/wife and compounds containing that separate modern lexeme.

primary_dictionary_text.text:
5200 jāmí 'related as brother and sister', m. 'brother', f. 'sister' RV., m. 'relative' RV., f. 'female relative, esp.
son's wife' MBh. Pk. jāmi - f. 'sister'; Kt. žämī́ 'wife's brother', Pr. imī́ (collides with imī́ < jā́mātr̥ -), Dm. Gaw. žamī́ ,
Kal. rumb. ǰōmī ; Sv. žamī́ 'wife's brother, sister's
husband', Phal. žamé ; K. zām f. 'husband's sister,
wife's brother's wife'; WPah. bhal. j̈aĩ f. 'husband's
sister'. — Ext. - l -: Kal. ǰhamili 'son's wife, woman';
Kho. ǰaméli 'daughter's son'; Bshk. ǰēmil 'husband's
sister'. jāmitvá-, jāmēya-; *jāmipati -. Addenda: jāmi-: M. j̈āv 'wife of husband's brother', Ko. j̈āva .

parents.Gloss: related as brother and sister; brother; sister; relative; female relative, esp. son's wife

proposals.evidence: Tentative l-extended member of the jāmí in-law family (CDIAL 5200), rather than a proven synchronic derivative of modern ẓami. Compare Kalasha ǰhamili son’s wife/woman and Gawri (Bashkarik) ǰēmil husband’s sister in Turner’s explicit -l extension. Perder žamili sister-in-law is coded husband’s sister, whereas the survey źāmili denotes brother’s wife (female ego) or husband’s brother’s wife. Preserve this semantic disagreement and the different sibilant spellings. Nuristani parallels support comparison but establish neither the exact suffix history nor borrowing direction.

approval: User: approve all; prefer Pashto where best matched, then Urdu for broadly Perso-Arabic terms. Approval includes qualified analyses, not a claim that uncertainties are resolved.
donor_policy: Prefer an attested Pashto donor where form and meaning fit best; otherwise prefer Urdu for broadly shared Perso-Arabic loans. Preserve explicit source attribution, phonological uncertainty and possible Nuristani mediation. Do not substitute a different dialect merely because its node is linkable.
